summary.overview: Myoglobin stores O2 in muscle; haemoglobin carries it in the blood. Both bind O2 at a haem Fe(II), but only haemoglobin, a cooperative tetramer regulated by allosteric effectors, can load O2 in the lungs and unload it in the tissues.

sections.heading: Haem and the O2-binding site
points: Haem is a protoporphyrin (four pyrrole rings) with an iron atom at the centre, bonded to the four pyrrole nitrogens.
Only Fe(II) binds O2. Fe(III), the met-form, cannot.
5th coordination bond: the proximal histidine. 6th position: O2 (empty in the deoxy form).
The distal histidine H-bonds bound O2, limits superoxide release and hinders CO binding.
When O2 binds, Fe moves into the plane of the porphyrin, pulling the proximal His and its α-helix with it.

sections.heading: Myoglobin vs haemoglobin
points: Myoglobin: one chain, in muscle. Hyperbolic curve, P50 ≈ 2 torr, so it acts as an O2 store.
Haemoglobin: an α2β2 tetramer (two αβ dimers) in red cells. Sigmoidal curve, P50 ≈ 26 torr, so it acts as a transporter.
Lungs (100 torr): Hb is ≈ 98% saturated. Active tissue (20 torr): ≈ 32%. So Hb delivers ≈ 66% of its O2, while myoglobin would deliver only ≈ 7%.

sections.heading: Cooperativity
points: T state (deoxy) = tense and low affinity. R state (oxy) = relaxed and high affinity.
Oxygenation rotates the α1β1 and α2β2 dimers by about 15° relative to each other.
Concerted model: the whole tetramer is either all-T or all-R. Sequential model: each binding raises its neighbours' affinity step by step.

sections.heading: Allosteric effectors
points: 2,3-BPG binds the central cavity of the T state only. It stabilises T and shifts the curve right (lower affinity). Its level rises at high altitude.
Bohr effect: H⁺ and CO2 lower O2 affinity. Protonated His and N-termini, and carbamates, stabilise T, so more O2 is released in active tissue.
Fetal Hb (α2γ2) has Ser in place of His143, so it binds 2,3-BPG weakly and has a higher affinity. This lets O2 pass from mother to fetus.
CO binds about 200× more tightly than O2 and pushes the remaining sites into R, so the O2 still bound is released poorly.

sections.heading: Abnormal haemoglobins
points: HbS (β6 Glu → Val): a sticky patch binds a pocket exposed only in deoxy (T) Hb, forming fibres and sickled cells.
α-thalassaemia: β4 tetramers (HbH) have high affinity and no cooperativity, so they deliver O2 poorly.
β-thalassaemia: unpaired α chains precipitate in red-cell precursors, causing anaemia.
Methaemoglobin (Fe³⁺) cannot carry O2, e.g. in nitrite poisoning of cattle (chocolate-brown blood).

keyTerms.definition: Protoporphyrin ring with a central Fe(II) that binds O2.
His forming the 5th coordination bond to the haem iron.
His that H-bonds bound O2 and hinders CO binding.
pO2 at which half the binding sites are occupied. Lower P50 = higher affinity.
Binding at one site increases the affinity of the other sites, giving a sigmoidal curve.
Tense (low-affinity, deoxy) and relaxed (high-affinity, oxy) quaternary states.
Red-cell allosteric effector that stabilises the T state and lowers O2 affinity.
Lower pH and higher CO2 reduce haemoglobin's O2 affinity.
Haemoglobin with Fe³⁺, which cannot bind O2.

examTips: Right shift = lower affinity = more O2 released (↑ 2,3-BPG, ↑ H⁺, ↑ CO2).
Myoglobin is a monomer: no cooperativity and no Bohr effect.
2,3-BPG binds the central cavity of the T state, not the haem.
CO does double damage: it occupies sites AND left-shifts the remaining ones.
HbS polymerises when DEoxygenated, because its binding pocket is exposed only in the T state.

questions.stem: Which bond does the proximal histidine of myoglobin form with the haem group?

options.text: The 5th coordination bond to the Fe(II) ion
options.why: The proximal His (F8) imidazole nitrogen occupies the 5th coordination position, below the porphyrin plane.

options.text: The 6th coordination bond to the Fe(II) ion
options.why: The 6th position is where O2 binds; it is empty in deoxymyoglobin.

options.text: A hydrogen bond to bound O2
options.why: That is the role of the distal histidine (E7), on the opposite side of the haem.

options.text: A covalent bond to one pyrrole nitrogen of the porphyrin
options.why: The four pyrrole nitrogens coordinate the iron; the histidine does not bond to the porphyrin ring itself.

questions.stem: Free haem in solution binds CO far more tightly than O2, yet inside myoglobin the preference for CO is much smaller. What accounts for this?

options.text: The distal histidine hinders the linear Fe–C–O geometry that CO prefers, and H-bonds bound O2
options.why: The distal His crowds the 6th site, forcing CO to bind at an unfavourable angle, while its H-bond stabilises bound O2.

options.text: The proximal histidine oxidises CO to CO2 before it can reach and bind the iron in the haem pocket
options.why: The proximal His is a ligand of the iron, not a redox catalyst; CO is not oxidised in the pocket.

options.text: The iron in myoglobin is in the Fe(III) state, which does not bind CO
options.why: Functional myoglobin contains Fe(II); Fe(III) (metmyoglobin) cannot bind O2 either.

options.text: 2,3-BPG occupies the CO binding site in myoglobin
options.why: 2,3-BPG binds only to the central cavity of the haemoglobin tetramer, not to myoglobin.

questions.stem: Cattle grazing nitrate-rich forage can develop nitrite poisoning, in which a large fraction of haemoglobin becomes methaemoglobin and the blood turns chocolate-brown. Why can methaemoglobin not carry oxygen?

options.text: The haem iron has been oxidised from Fe(II) to Fe(III), which does not bind O2
options.why: Only ferrous iron binds O2 reversibly. Nitrite oxidises it to ferric iron, giving methaemoglobin.

options.text: Nitrite displaces the proximal histidine, so the iron falls out of the porphyrin
options.why: The iron stays in the haem; the defect is its oxidation state, not its loss.

options.text: Nitrite binds the 2,3-BPG pocket and locks the tetramer in the R state
options.why: Locking in R would raise O2 affinity, not abolish binding, and this is not the mechanism of methaemoglobinaemia.

options.text: Nitrite hydrolyses the globin chains, releasing free haem
options.why: The globin remains intact; the change is at the iron atom.

questions.stem: The haem groups in haemoglobin are 24–40 Å apart, so they cannot interact directly. What is the first structural event that links O2 binding at one haem to the affinity of the other subunits?

options.text: The Fe moves into the porphyrin plane, pulling the proximal His and its helix, which shifts the αβ interface
options.why: Iron movement drags the F-helix; the helix's C-terminal end lies at the α1β1/α2β2 interface and favours the T→R transition.

options.text: Bound O2 diffuses through the protein to the neighbouring haem groups and binds them in turn
options.why: O2 stays bound at its site; communication is through protein conformation, not ligand transfer.

options.text: Electrons flow between the haem groups through the porphyrin rings, changing each iron's charge
options.why: There is no electron transfer pathway between haems; the effect is conformational.

options.text: O2 binding releases a proton that travels to the other haems and directly protonates their iron
options.why: Bohr protons are released from His and N-termini, not haems, and that is a consequence, not the trigger.

questions.stem: Myoglobin has P50 ≈ 2 torr and a hyperbolic binding curve, Y = pO2 / (pO2 + P50). If blood carried myoglobin instead of haemoglobin, roughly what fraction of its O2 would be released between the lungs (100 torr) and active tissue (20 torr)?

options.text: About 7%
options.why: Y(100) = 100/102 ≈ 0.98 and Y(20) = 20/22 ≈ 0.91, so only ≈ 7% is unloaded — far less than the ≈ 66% unloaded by haemoglobin.

options.text: About 66%
options.why: That is the value for cooperative haemoglobin (98% → 32%), not myoglobin.

options.text: About 50%
options.why: 50% saturation occurs at P50 = 2 torr, far below both pressures given.

options.text: About 90%
options.why: 90% is close to myoglobin's saturation at 20 torr, not the amount released.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes the concerted (MWC) model of cooperative O2 binding?

options.text: All subunits are in the T state or all in the R state; ligand binding shifts the equilibrium between them
options.why: In the concerted model, the tetramer switches as a unit; each bound O2 makes the all-R form more probable.

options.text: Each bound O2 changes only its own subunit, which raises the affinity of neighbouring subunits step by step
options.why: That is the sequential (KNF) model, in which mixed T/R tetramers exist.

options.text: O2 binding converts R-state subunits into T-state subunits
options.why: The direction is reversed: O2 favours R (high affinity); deoxyhaemoglobin is T.

options.text: Subunits bind O2 independently, and cooperativity arises from 2,3-BPG binding
options.why: Independent sites give a hyperbolic curve; 2,3-BPG modulates affinity but is not the source of cooperativity.

questions.stem: How is the quaternary structure of adult haemoglobin A best described?

options.text: A pair of identical αβ dimers (α1β1 and α2β2)
options.why: HbA is α2β2, organised as two αβ protomers; their interface changes most on oxygenation.

options.text: Four identical α chains
options.why: HbA has two α and two β chains; β4 tetramers (HbH) occur in α-thalassaemia.

options.text: A single chain with four haem-binding domains
options.why: Haemoglobin is a tetramer of four separate polypeptides, each with one haem.

options.text: Two α chains and two γ chains
options.why: α2γ2 is fetal haemoglobin (HbF), not the adult form.

questions.stem: On oxygenation, how does the quaternary structure of haemoglobin change?

options.text: The α1β1 and α2β2 dimers rotate about 15° relative to each other
options.why: The T→R transition is a rotation of one αβ dimer relative to the other, altering the dimer–dimer interface.

options.text: The tetramer dissociates into four free monomers, each like myoglobin
options.why: Haemoglobin remains a tetramer; dissociation would abolish cooperativity.

options.text: The α-helices of each subunit unfold and refold into β-sheets
options.why: Secondary structure is preserved; the change is a rigid-body quaternary rearrangement.

options.text: The α1 and β1 subunits separate while α2 and β2 stay bound
options.why: The αβ dimers stay intact; it is the interface between the two dimers that shifts.

questions.stem: After several days at high altitude, red-cell 2,3-BPG rises. What is the effect on haemoglobin's O2-binding curve?

options.text: It shifts to the right (P50 increases), favouring O2 release in tissues
options.why: 2,3-BPG binds the central cavity of the T state only, stabilising T and lowering O2 affinity.

options.text: It shifts to the left (P50 decreases), favouring O2 loading in the lungs
options.why: A left shift would result from removing 2,3-BPG, not adding it.

options.text: It becomes hyperbolic because cooperativity is lost
options.why: 2,3-BPG shifts the curve but haemoglobin remains cooperative.

options.text: It does not change because 2,3-BPG binds at the haem iron
options.why: 2,3-BPG binds a site distinct from the haem — the definition of an allosteric effector.

questions.stem: Fetal haemoglobin (α2γ2) has a higher O2 affinity than maternal HbA in the same red-cell environment. What is the molecular basis?

options.text: Ser replaces His143 in the γ chain, removing positive charges from the 2,3-BPG site
options.why: Fewer positive charges lining the central cavity weaken 2,3-BPG binding, so the T state is less stabilised and affinity rises.

options.text: The γ chain lacks a distal histidine, so O2 can bind more tightly to the haem iron
options.why: The distal His is conserved; the difference lies in the 2,3-BPG binding pocket.

options.text: Fetal red cells contain no 2,3-BPG at all, because the placenta removes it from blood
options.why: 2,3-BPG is present; it is the haemoglobin's affinity for it that is lower.

options.text: HbF is a monomer like myoglobin and therefore non-cooperative
options.why: HbF is a cooperative tetramer.

questions.stem: In hard-working skeletal muscle, pH falls and pCO2 rises. How does this affect O2 delivery?

options.text: O2 affinity falls, because protonated His and N-terminal groups, and carbamates, stabilise the T state
options.why: This is the Bohr effect: H+ and CO2 both favour deoxyhaemoglobin, so more O2 is unloaded where it is needed.

options.text: O2 affinity rises, because H⁺ binds the haem iron and holds the O2 more tightly in the pocket
options.why: H+ binds globin residues, not the iron, and lowers affinity.

options.text: CO2 competes with O2 for the haem iron, so less O2 can be carried from the lungs to the muscle
options.why: CO2 binds N-terminal amino groups as carbamate, not the iron.

options.text: There is no effect, because pH changes only affect myoglobin
options.why: The Bohr effect is a property of tetrameric haemoglobin, not myoglobin.

questions.stem: A dog is rescued from a kennel fire with 40% carboxyhaemoglobin. Why is tissue oxygenation worse than in a dog with a 40% reduction in haemoglobin (anaemia)?

options.text: CO on one subunit shifts the others toward the R state, so their O2 is held tightly and released poorly
options.why: Besides occupying sites, CO left-shifts the curve of the remaining haem groups, impairing unloading in tissues.

options.text: CO oxidises the haem irons to Fe(III), so the haemoglobin can no longer carry any oxygen at all
options.why: CO binds Fe(II); oxidation to Fe(III) describes methaemoglobin.

options.text: CO binds 2,3-BPG and removes it from the red cells, so haemoglobin becomes locked in the T state
options.why: CO binds the haem iron, not 2,3-BPG.

options.text: CO makes haemoglobin release O2 too easily in the lungs
options.why: The problem is poor release in tissues, not in the lungs.

questions.stem: Why does haemoglobin S polymerise mainly when it is deoxygenated?

options.text: The β6 Val sticky patch binds a hydrophobic pocket (Phe85, Leu88) exposed only in the T state
options.why: In oxyHbS (R state) Phe85 and Leu88 are buried, so the Val patch has no partner and fibres do not form.

options.text: Deoxygenation exposes the mutant valine, which is buried inside the protein in the R state
options.why: Val6 is on the surface in both states; it is the complementary pocket that is T-state specific.

options.text: The Glu→Val substitution adds a negative charge that repels O2, so HbS stays deoxygenated longer
options.why: Glu is negative and Val is uncharged, so the mutation removes a negative charge.

options.text: Deoxygenated HbS forms disulfide bonds between β chains, which link the molecules into long fibres
options.why: The aggregation is driven by hydrophobic contacts, not disulfide bonds.

questions.stem: In α-thalassaemia, excess β chains form β4 tetramers (HbH). Why does HbH deliver O2 poorly to tissues?

options.text: It binds O2 with high affinity and no cooperativity, so little O2 is released at tissue pO2
options.why: Without α–β interfaces there is no T→R switch; HbH behaves like myoglobin.

options.text: It cannot bind O2 at all, because unpaired β chains are made without their haem groups
options.why: β chains contain haem and bind O2.

options.text: It precipitates in red-cell precursors in the marrow before the cells can reach the blood
options.why: Precipitation of unpaired α chains is the problem in β-thalassaemia.

options.text: It is very sensitive to 2,3-BPG and stays locked in the T state, so it picks up little O2
options.why: A T-locked tetramer would release O2 too readily, not too little.

questions.stem: Diving mammals such as seals have very high myoglobin concentrations in their skeletal muscle. What is the main advantage?

options.text: Myoglobin stores O2 in the muscle and releases it only when intracellular pO2 falls very low
options.why: With P50 ≈ 2 torr, myoglobin stays loaded until muscle pO2 becomes very low, then acts as a reserve.

options.text: Myoglobin carries O2 from the lungs to the muscles through the blood, like a second haemoglobin
options.why: Myoglobin is intracellular; haemoglobin performs blood transport.

options.text: Myoglobin binds CO2 and buffers the lactic acid made during the dive through the Bohr effect
options.why: Myoglobin, being monomeric, shows no significant Bohr effect.

options.text: Its cooperative binding lets it unload most of its O2 at the moderate pO2 of resting muscle
options.why: Myoglobin is not cooperative; its curve is hyperbolic.

options.text: In the central cavity between the β subunits, a pocket present only in the T state
options.why: The positively charged cavity binds the highly anionic 2,3-BPG and collapses on transition to R.

options.text: At the sixth coordination site of each haem iron, in place of the bound O2
options.why: That site binds O2 or CO, not 2,3-BPG.

options.text: At the distal histidine of each α subunit, inside the pocket where O2 binds
options.why: The distal His lines the O2 pocket, which is unrelated to 2,3-BPG.

options.text: On the outer surface of the β chains, at the same site as the HbS valine
options.why: 2,3-BPG binds inside the central cavity, not on the surface.

flashcards.front: Which oxidation state of haem iron binds O2?
flashcards.back: Fe(II), ferrous. Fe(III) (met-form) does not bind O2.
Proximal His: 5th coordination bond to Fe. Distal His: H-bonds bound O2, limits superoxide release and hinders CO binding.
Myoglobin ≈ 2 torr (high affinity, hyperbolic). Haemoglobin ≈ 26 torr (sigmoidal, cooperative).
T (tense) = deoxyHb, constrained, low affinity. R (relaxed) = oxyHb, high affinity.
Concerted: whole tetramer is all-T or all-R. Sequential: each binding raises neighbours' affinity without a full T→R switch.

flashcards.front: Hb saturation in lungs vs active tissue?
flashcards.back: ≈ 98% at 100 torr, ≈ 32% at 20 torr, so ≈ 66% of the O2 is delivered.
Binds the T-state central cavity, stabilises T, lowers O2 affinity (right shift). Without it, Hb would release only ≈ 8% of its O2.

flashcards.front: Bohr effect: two ways CO2 lowers O2 affinity?
flashcards.back: 1) Forms carbonic acid, so pH falls and His/N-termini are protonated. 2) Forms carbamates on N-terminal amino groups, stabilising T.

flashcards.front: Why does HbF have higher O2 affinity than HbA?
flashcards.back: γ-chain Ser replaces β His143, so 2,3-BPG binds weakly, T is less stabilised and affinity is higher.
β6 Glu → Val. The hydrophobic patch binds Phe85/Leu88 of a neighbouring T-state Hb, forming fibres when deoxygenated.
α: too little α chain, β4 (HbH) forms with high affinity and no cooperativity. β: too little β chain, α chains precipitate in RBC precursors, causing anaemia (Cooley's anaemia).

flashcards.front: Two ways CO harms O2 transport?
flashcards.back: Binds Fe(II) ≈ 200× more tightly than O2, and shifts the remaining subunits to R so they release O2 poorly.
